title: How a logistics company should write an about page
metaTitle: Logistics about page: name the desk
excerpt: Name who quotes, who handles an exception, and the rules that change an operator's risk. Keep the founding story only if it explains a rule you still keep.
alt: A bright office window ledge with a laptop, a closed notebook, white chairs, and a tall indoor tree, a real room for a page that should name real people.
caption: A bright window ledge with a laptop, a notebook, and a tall indoor tree. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a logistics about page prove?
faqs.answer: It should prove who answers when a receiver refuses a trailer or an appointment slips. Name the role, the hours, and one or two rules you actually follow, such as calling before you roll a window you set. A mission statement and a photo of a container do not answer that.

faqs.question: When should we tell the company origin story?
faqs.answer: Tell it when it explains a boundary you still enforce, in one paragraph, then return to the quote path. A timeline of trucks, cities, and rebrands is optional. If removing the story removes no rule and no name the operator needs, it belongs in an anniversary note, not on this page.

faqs.question: Should a small carrier hide the size of the team?
faqs.answer: State who answers and when, including after hours. A night number that reaches a person is a clearer promise than an implied national account team. Update the names when people change. An about page that lists someone who has left is a failed introduction.

markdown:
The logistics company about page should prove that specific people stand behind the freight. Name who does the work, and why an operator with a deadline should care. Skip the origin story unless it changes the decision to request a quote.

A skyline and a sentence about passion for logistics do not answer the question the operator actually has. Who picks up the phone when the receiver refuses the trailer?

## Name the desk

The first screen should name the accountable roles. Who quotes. Who dispatches after hours. Who handles a claim. Use real names when those people are willing to be called. If they are not, name the role and the hours without a stock portrait in a vest.

An operator is handing you freight they may not see again until a POD exists. They want a person who has stood on a dock, not a brand film. "Quotes are answered by the desk until 5pm Central. After that, the on-call dispatcher takes exceptions." That paragraph is the about page doing its job.

Google's people-first guidance treats first-hand experience as a reason to trust a page. Here the experience is operational. Years on a dock, a region you have run through weather, a claims process you have actually closed. "We live and breathe supply chain" is not experience. "We still call the receiver before the truck leaves the terminal" is experience, if it is true this month.

If the company is small, say so in the same breath as the coverage. A night number that reaches a person is a stronger about page than a headcount you hope to have next year. Do not borrow a team from a stock library. Operators can tell, and the tell is fatal on a page that exists to prove someone is real.

## Why this operator should care

Translate character into rules that change their risk.

You do not reclass a shipment without a photo and a call. You do not roll an appointment you set, without telling them before the window. You send the exception to the person who booked, not only to a portal they will not check at 6pm. Each rule is a sentence. Each sentence needs an owner, even if the owner is a role.

These lines belong on the about page because they are about judgment, not about a product feature. The services page says what you haul. The about page says how you behave when the haul goes wrong. Both have to match. A service block that promises a same-day POD and an about page that never mentions documents is a gap a careful coordinator will feel.

If the founder is still the person who answers, say that without a speech. "You get the owner on exceptions until we have a second dispatcher." The right shippers will hear reliability. The wrong ones, who need a national account team, will look elsewhere. That filter is worth more than a paragraph about humble beginnings.

Keep mission language to a line, after the rules. A mission can be sincere. It does not move a pallet.

## When the first truck belongs on the page

An origin story earns its place when it explains a rule you still keep. You started as a carrier that was tired of silent email, so a human still confirms the appointment. You started in one city, so you do not pretend to be a forty-eight-state network. The story is evidence. It is not the introduction.

One paragraph. What you did. What went wrong in the market you came from. What you refuse to repeat. Then back to the quote path. A timeline of acquisitions and rebrands is a corporate biography. Most operators do not need it in order to tender a load. If a merger changed the name on the invoice, say the name they will see, which is a fact, not a saga.

Delete the story as a test. If the operator lost no rule and no name, the story was for the anniversary post. Put it there.

## What to leave off the about page

Values words that any carrier could print. A map with a pin in every state you once emailed. Awards that require a footnote to mean anything. Software logos that imply a tracking product you do not operate. Photographs of containers that are not your containers.

Investor and association marks belong only when the operator would read them as a safety fact. A specific insurance limit they asked for in the last ten RFPs can be a sentence. A badge that says "excellence" cannot.

Do not invent a customer quotation about your culture. If a shipper will say, in their words, that you called before you rolled a missed appointment, and they will stand by the sentence, use it with permission. If they will not, write the rule yourself and skip the quotation marks.

Press about a rebrand is not proof you can move freight. A short note that the legal name on the bill of lading matches the name on the site is more useful than a clipping.

## The week, written plainly

Describe a normal week in a few sentences. When quotes stop. How an after-hours exception is escalated. What "we will call you" means if the first number does not answer. Which time zone the clocks use. This is more convincing than a culture section because it can be checked.

Write the week you are in. When you hire a night desk, change the sentence the week they start. An about page that still names a dispatcher who left is a broken introduction. Someone will call that name.

Facilities can be mentioned when they change the work. A cross-dock with stated hours. A yard that can hold a drop trailer. An office that is not where the freight is, if that would otherwise surprise someone who shows up. Address theater, a prestigious mailbox with no one at it, does not belong.

If you mention technology, tie it to a behavior on the week. Status emails at pickup and delivery. A portal the booker can share with a receiver. Leave the architecture diagram out. The operator is not buying your stack.

## Point them at a quote

End on request a quote, with the same label as the homepage, and the short list of facts to have ready. The about page is not a dead end after the feelings. The person who just learned who answers at night is ready to send a lane.

Repeat only the promises you can keep this month. If the about page says two hours and the contact page says a business day, fix one of them before you add a portrait. Contradiction on this page is worse than thin copy, because you used the page to claim accountability.

## Test the page against a bad afternoon

Walk a real exception, with names removed, through the sentences you wrote. Receiver closed early. Driver held past free time. Weight came in heavy. Who did the page say would call, and did that person call? If the page and the afternoon disagree, change the page. Do not write a more inspiring version of the afternoon.

Ask a coordinator who is not on your staff to read only the about page and tell you three things. Who they would phone at 6pm. One thing you will not do to their freight. What they should include in a quote. Missing answers become sentences. Answers they invented from the photographs mean the photographs are doing too much and the sentences too little.

Check the clocks, the time zone, and the legal name against the invoice and the contact page in the same sitting. The about page is where inconsistency looks like a company that will be hard to reach when the freight is already on a yard. Fix the words before you commission a film.

Keep one shared note for the facts that appear in more than one place: hours, time zone, legal name, after-hours number, and the two rules you are willing to be judged on. The about page, the quote confirmation, and the signature on an email should draw from that note. When a fact changes, it changes once. A logistics company that publishes three different clocks will spend its reputation explaining which clock was meant.

If you add a photograph, caption it with the role and the place, not with a slogan. A dispatcher at a named terminal is evidence. A driver on an unnamed highway is a costume, even when the light is good. The caption is part of the proof that someone stands behind the freight. If you cannot write the caption without the word passionate, choose a different frame. A plain caption a dispatcher would accept is the standard.

A named desk still has to show a load that tested it. The next piece is [proof pages for a logistics company](/blog/proof-pages-for-a-logistics-company), where a constraint and a decision replace a group photo.
